abla_	au z(\Phi^t x) , 
abla_	au z(\Phi^t x) angle_	au = 0 + \alpha\omega = \alpha\omega. \] Thus $\alpha=1$ as claimed. This means that the gradient vector field $
abla_	au z$ is invariant under the flow, namely, \[\Phi^t_*|_x 
abla_	au z(x) = 
abla_	au z(\Phi^t x), \quad  orall x\in M. \] Therefore, since $	ilde{V}$ is a linear combination of the two flow invariant vector fields $V$ and $
abla_	au z$, $	ilde{V}$ is also invariant under $\Phi^t$. We summarize all these invariances below.  egin{equation} \Phi^t_*|_x 	ilde{V}(x) = 	ilde{V}(\Phi^t x), \quad \Phi^t_*|_x V(x) = V(\Phi^t x), \quad \Phi^t_*|_x 
abla_	au z(x) = 
abla_	au z(\Phi^t x), \quad  orall x\in M. \end{equation} We will next show that the two flows commute, i.e., $	ilde{\Phi}^t \Phi^s $ = $\Phi^s 	ilde{\Phi}^{t}$ for every $s,t\ineal$. Let $x\in M$, and define $x'(s) := 	ilde{\Phi}^s(x)$, $x''(s) := \Phi^t(x''(s))$ and $x'''(s) := 	ilde{\Phi}^{-s}(x'(s))$. We have to show that $x'''(s) = \Phi^t(x)$ for every $s\ineal$. Since this is true for $s=0$, it is equivalent to prove that $ rac{d}{ds} x'''(s) = 0$. This follows from \[ egin{split}  rac{d}{ds} x'''(s) &=  rac{d}{ds} 	ilde{\Phi}^{-s} \Phi^t 	ilde{\Phi}^s(x) =  rac{d}{du}|_{u=s} 	ilde{\Phi}^{-u} \Phi^t 	ilde{\Phi}^s(x) +  rac{d}{dv}|_{v=s} 	ilde{\Phi}^{-s} \Phi^t 	ilde{\Phi}^v(x) \ &= -	ilde{V}(x'''(s)) + 	ilde{\Phi}^{-s}_*|_{x''(s)} \Phi^t_*|_{x'(s)} 	ilde{V}(x'(s)) \ & = -	ilde{V}(x'''(s)) + 	ilde{\Phi}^{-s}_*|_{x''(s)} 	ilde{V}(x''(s)), \quad \mbox{by } \eqref{eqn:inv_vector}, \ & = -	ilde{V}(x'''(s)) + 	ilde{V}(x'''(s)) = 0. \end{split}\] The last equality above again follows from the invariance of the vector field $	ilde{V}$ under the flow $	ilde{\Phi}^t$ that it generates. This completes the proof of Claim~(ii). This completes the proof of Theorem~ef{thm:fol_1D_flow}. See Figure~ef{fig:comm_flow} for an illustration. \qed
nodes.statement_short: <V, grad z> = omega gives tangency; flow invariance of V and grad z gives invariance of tilde V; commutation by differentiating the conjugated flow.

nodes.name: Flow preserves its generator
nodes.statement: V(\Phi^t(x)) = d/ds|_{s=t} \Phi^s(x) = d/ds|_{s=0} \Phi^{t+s}(x) = \Phi^t_* (x)V(x) .
nodes.label: eqn:Flow_commut_Gen

nodes.name: Invariance of vector fields
nodes.statement: \Phi^t_*|_x \tilde{V}(x) = \tilde{V}(\Phi^t x), \quad \Phi^t_*|_x V(x) = V(\Phi^t x), \quad \Phi^t_*|_x \nabla_\tau z(x) = \nabla_\tau z(\Phi^t x), \quad \forall x\in M.
nodes.label: eqn:inv_vector

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (laminar flow eigen-properties)
nodes.statement:
The proof of Claim~(i) is analogous to the proof of Theorem~ef{thm:fol_1D_basic}~(iii), and will be omitted. We next prove Claim~(iv). By \eqref{def:tildeV} we have \[ V \zeta = 	ilde{V} \zeta + \omega 
abla_	au z \zeta . \] The first differential operator acts only along the tangent subspaces of the leaves of $z$. The second differential operator acts along the vector field normal to the flow. Due to the local product structure, \[ V \zeta = \iota \omega' \zeta + \iota \omega z \zeta . \] Thus $\zeta$ satisfies the eigenfunction equation with eigenfrequency $\omega + \omega'$. If $	ilde\zeta$ is a $C^r$ eigenfunction, then so is $\zeta$. Suppose $	ilde\zeta$ is an $L^2(	ilde{\mu})$ eigenfunction. By Theorem ef{thm:fol_1D_basic}~(iii) , since the flow $\Phi^t$ preserves the conditional measures of $\mu$ along the fibres of $\mathcal{F}$, the set $M'$ on which the eigenvalue equation holds has full $\mu$-measure. Thus, $\zeta$ is an $L^2(\mu)$ eigenfunction. By Lemma ef{lem:submersion}, the $d$ vector fields $
abla_	au z_1, \ldots, 
abla_	au z_d$ are linearly independent everywhere on $M$, for any choice of a Riemannian metric $	au$. Thus $	au$ can be chosen so that these vector fields are mutually orthogonal and each of constant unit norm. As a result, using the identity \eqref{def:grad_diff_Lie} for the gradient, we get \[ 	ilde{V}(z_j) = V(z_j) - \omega 
abla_{	au} z_1(z_j) = \iota \omega_j z_j - i \omega \langle 
abla_{	au} z_1 , 
abla_{	au} z_j angle_{	au} z_j = \iota \omega_j z_j, \quad j=2,\ldots,d . \] This completes the proof of Claim~(iii) and of Theorem~ef{thm:fol_1D_flow_eig}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Split V into tilde V plus the gradient term to get the eigenvalue equation; choose an orthonormalizing metric via Lemma 1 for claim (iii).

nodes.name: Plan: induction for (i)-(v)
nodes.statement: We first prove Claims (i)-- (v). The proof will be by induction.
nodes.statement_short: Claims (i)-(v) by induction on k.

nodes.name: Base case k=1
nodes.statement: We first check the base case corresponding to $k=1$. In this case, claims (i) and (iii) follow from Theorem \ref{thm:fol_1D_flow}~(i); claim (ii) follows from Theorem \ref{thm:fol_1D_flow_eig}~(iii); claim (iv) follows from Theorem \ref{thm:fol_1D_flow}~(iv); claim (v) follows Theorem \ref{thm:fol_1D_flow_eig}~(i).
nodes.statement_short: Base case from Theorems 4 and 5.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Next we verify the inductive step. So lets assume that the statement is true for every $k$ in the range $1\leq k \leq \bar{k}$ for some $1\leq \bar{k}<d$. Note that now $V_{\bar{k}}$ restricts to a vector field on $\calL_k$, which we can interpret as its own dynamical system. We can now construct a vector field $\tilde{V}_{\bar{k}}$ as in \eqref{def:tildeV}, which coincides with $V_{\bar{k}+1}$. The relation between $V_{\bar{k}+1}$ and $V_{\bar{k}}$ as listed in Theorems \ref{thm:fol_1D_flow} and \ref{thm:fol_1D_flow_eig} now complete the inductive step.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the tilde-V construction to V_k restricted to L_k, which yields V_{k+1}.

nodes.name: Take an eigenvalue of R_d
nodes.statement: We next prove Claim (vi). Take any eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $R_d$. Again by unitarity, we have $\lambda = e^{\iota \omega'}$ for some eigenfrequency $\omega'$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix an eigenvalue lambda = e^{i omega'} of R_d.

nodes.name: Lift eigenvalue to flow eigenfrequency
nodes.statement: Then by Theorem \ref{thm:fol_1D_basemap} and \eqref{eqn:def:tensor_with_base_map}, the flow $\Phi_d^t | \calL_{d-1}$ must have $\frac{\omega_{d} \omega'}{2\pi}$ as an eigenfrequency. By Theorem \ref{thm:fol_1D_flow_eig}~(ii), the flow $\Phi_{d-1}^t | \calL_{d-2}$ must have $\frac{\omega_{d} \omega'}{2\pi} + \omega_{d-1}$ as an eigenfrequency. Continuing this way, we get $\frac{\omega_{d} \omega'}{2\pi} + \omega_{d-1} + \cdots + \omega_1$ to be an eigenfrequency for the original flow.
nodes.statement_short: Theorems 2 and 5 lift it to an eigenfrequency of the original flow.

nodes.name: Use generating assumption and independence
nodes.statement: By Assumption \ref{A:generating}, there must be integers $a_1, \ldots, a_d$ such that \[\frac{\omega_{d} \omega'}{2\pi} + \omega_{d-1} + \cdots + \omega_1 = a_1 \omega_1 + \cdots + a_k \omega_d .\] By the Independence of the generating frequencies, this is only possible if $\omega'/2\pi$ is an integer.
nodes.statement_short: By Assumption 3 and independence, omega'/2pi is an integer.

nodes.name: Conclude weak mixing
nodes.statement: But this would mean that $\lambda=1$ a trivial eigenvalue for the return map. Thus the return map has no non-trivial eigenvalues and must be weakly mixing. The statements about weak or strong mixing, and their rates, now directly follow from Theorem \ref{thm:fol_1D_return}~(iii). This completes the proof of claim (v) and also of Theorem \ref{thm:Main}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: So lambda=1, R_d is weakly mixing, and mixing statements follow from Theorem 3 (iii).

nodes.name: Inverse Xi of Psi^(d)
nodes.statement: Since $\Psi^{(d)}$ is a bijection, it has an inverse $\Xi$ whose components $\Xi_L : M \to \calL_d$ and $\Xi_T : M\to [0,1)^d$ are defined uniquely by the relation below : \begin{equation} \Xi_L(z) = x, \; \Xi_T(x) = (t_1,\ldots,t_d) \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \Psi^{(d)}(x,t_1,\ldots,t_d) = z, \end{equation} The following commutative diagram summarizes the relationship between $\Psi^{(d)}$, $\Xi$, $\Xi_L$ and $\Xi_T$. \[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep = huge, row sep = large] M \arrow{r}{\Xi_L} \arrow{d}[swap]{\Xi_T} \arrow[shift left=2]{dr}{\Xi} & \calL_d \\ \ [0,1) & \ [0,1)^d \times \calL_d \arrow{l}{\proj_T} \arrow{u}[swap]{\proj_L} \arrow[shift left=2]{ul}{\Psi^{(d)}} \end{tikzcd}\]
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the inverse Xi of Psi^(d) and its components.

nodes.name: Construct Gamma^t
nodes.statement: Equipped with these notations, we can construct the flow $\Gamma^t$ indicated below. \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} [row sep = large] M \arrow{rr}{ \Phi^t } & & M \arrow{d}[swap]{\Xi} \\ \calL_d \times [0,1)^d \arrow{u}{ \Psi^{(d)} } \arrow[dashed]{rr}[swap]{\Gamma^t} & & \calL_d \times [0,1)^d \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} The dashed arrow indicates that the arrow is defined as the composition along the upper loop. This leads to an automatic satisfaction of the commutation.
nodes.statement_short: Define Gamma^t as the conjugate of Phi^t by Psi^(d).

nodes.name: Verify the flow property
nodes.statement: To verify that $\Gamma^t$ is indeed a flow, we have to verify that for any $t,s\in \real$, $\Gamma^{t+s} = \Gamma^t \circ \Gamma^s$. This follows from the commuting diagram below : \[\begin{tikzcd} [row sep = large] M \arrow[dashed, bend left=30]{rrrr}{\Phi^{t+s}} \arrow{rr}{ \Phi^t } & & M \arrow[bend right=30]{d}[swap]{\Xi} \arrow{rr}{ \Phi^t } & & M \arrow{d}[swap]{\Xi} \\ \calL_d \times [0,1)^d \arrow[dashed, bend right=30]{rrrr}[swap]{\Gamma^{t+s}} \arrow{u}{ \Psi^{(d)} } \arrow[dashed]{rr}[swap]{\Gamma^t} & & \calL_d \times [0,1)^d \arrow[bend right=30]{u}[swap]{ \Psi^{(d)} } \arrow[dashed]{rr}[swap]{\Gamma^s} & & \calL_d \times [0,1)^d \end{tikzcd}\] The two commuting squares on the left and right, as well as the square formed by the periphery, follow from \eqref{eqn:def:Gamma_t}. The middle loop created by the two opposite arrows hold since they represent inverses. The commutation in the upper loop holds because $\Phi^t$ is a flow. These five commutations come together to create the larger commutation diagram above. The consequence is the lower commutation loop, which is exactly the flow equation.
nodes.statement_short: Verify Gamma^{t+s} = Gamma^t Gamma^s by diagram chasing.

nodes.name: Explicit form of Gamma^t
nodes.statement: In spite of the vague nature of $\Phi^t$, the flow $\Gamma^t$ has a more explicit format : \begin{equation} \begin{split} \theta_1 &\mapsto \theta_1 + t\omega_1 \\ \theta_2 &\mapsto \theta_1 + \theta_2 + t\omega_2 \\ \vdots &\mapsto \vdots \\ \theta_d &\mapsto \theta_1 + \cdots + \theta_d + t \omega_d \\ y &\mapsto \paran{\Xi_L \circ \Phi^t \circ \Psi^{(d)}} \paran{ y, \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_d } \end{split} , \end{equation} for each $y\in \calL_d$ and $\paran{ \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_d } \in [0,1)^d $.
nodes.statement_short: Write Gamma^t explicitly as a skew product.

nodes.name: Change of angular variables
nodes.statement: Note that the change of variables \[ \paran{\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_d} \mapsto \paran{ \theta_1, \theta_1 + \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_1 + \cdots + \theta_d } , \] converts \eqref{eqn:skew:1} into \eqref{eqn:def:qpd}, thus proving the claim of Corollary \ref{corr:skew}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: A linear change of angles converts the skew product to the q.p.d. form.

nodes.name: Spectral correspondence via conjugacy
nodes.statement: Corollary \ref{corr:spectral_charac} relies on the fact that $\Psi^{(d)}$ is an invertible and measure preserving transformation between the two $\Phi^t$ and $\Gamma^t$. Thus there is a one-to-one correspondence between the discrete and continuous spectra of the two flows.
nodes.statement_short: Psi^(d) is a measure-preserving conjugacy, so spectra correspond.

nodes.name: Angular functions span D
nodes.statement: According to the skew product nature of \eqref{eqn:skew:1}, the functions on $\calL_D \times [0,1)^d$ which only depend on the angular coordinates $[0,1)^k$ must lie in $\Disc$. Note that these functions have a set of $d$ generating functions. By Assumption \ref{A:generating} which we have included, this space is also maximal.
nodes.statement_short: Functions of angular coordinates lie in D and by Assumption 3 are all of it.

nodes.name: Explicit splitting
nodes.statement: Thus the space $\Disc$ is indeed the space $L^2 \paran{ [0,1)^d; \Leb }$. In that case its orthogonal component must be the space $L^2 \paran{ \calL_d; \mu_d }$. Equation \eqref{eqn:spectral_charac}, \eqref{eqn:Td_translate} describes how these functional spaces on $\calL_d\times [0,1)^d$ map back into $L^2(\mu)$. The decomposition $L^2(\mu) = \Disc \oplus \Disc^\bot$ from \eqref{eqn:L2_decomp} can now be explicitly written as \begin{equation} \Disc := \left\{ f\circ \Xi_T \;:\; f\in L^2 \paran{ [0,1)^d; \Leb } \right\} , \quad \Disc^\bot := \left\{ f\circ\Xi_L \;:\; f \in L^2 \paran{ \calL_d; \mu_d } \right\} . \end{equation} This completes the proof of the Corollary. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Identify D and its complement explicitly.

nodes.name: Claims (i) and (ii)
nodes.statement: Claim~(i) is a direct consequence of \eqref{eqn:Def_koop_eigen}, and Claim~(ii) follows from Claim~(i).
nodes.statement_short: Claims (i),(ii) follow directly from the eigenfunction equation.

nodes.name: Notation Borel and T
nodes.statement: Let $\Borel(A)$ denote the Borel $\sigma$-algebras of of a topological space $A$. Now define $T:= 2\pi/\omega$, so that \[ \Phi^{sT} : \mathcal{F}_{\theta} \mapsto \mathcal{F}_{\theta+2s\pi \bmod 2\pi} , \quad \forall s\in\real, \quad \forall\theta\in S^1, \] and $X = \sqcup_{s\in [0,1)} \mathcal{F}_{2s\pi}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce Borel sigma-algebras and the period T = 2pi/omega.

nodes.name: Define averaged measure nu
nodes.statement:
For the proof of Claim~(iii), define a Borel measure $
u$ on $\calL_1$ as follows. \[
u:= A\mapsto \int_0^1 \left(\mu|\mathcal{F}_{2s\pi}ight)\left(\Phi^{sT} Aight)ds, \quad  orall A\in \Borel \paran{ \calL_1 }.\] In other words, given a measurable subset $A$ of the base leaf $\calL_1$, $
u(A)$ is the average of the conditional measures $\mu|\mathcal{F}_{2s\pi}$ on the images $\Phi^{sT} A \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{2s\pi}$. The first important observation is the following.  egin{equation} \mu\left(\Psi\left(A	imes [0,1)ight)ight) = 
u(A), \quad  orall A\in \Borel(L). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define nu on L_1 as the average of pushed-back conditional measures and state (23).

nodes.name: Verify (23)
nodes.statement: To see why \eqref{eqn:product_mes_tower} holds, note that the set $S$ = $\Psi\left(A\times [0,1)\right)$ is the union $\cup_{s\in [0,1)} \Phi^{sT}(A)$. Thus by the definition of the conditional measures $\mu|\mathcal{F}_{2s\pi}$, \[\mu\left(S\right) = \int_X 1_Sd\mu = \int_0^1 ds\int_{\mathcal{F}_{2s\pi}} 1_S d(\mu|\mathcal{F}_{2s\pi}) = \int_0^1 \left(\mu|\mathcal{F}_{2s\pi}\right)\left(\Phi^{sT} A\right)ds = \nu(A).\]
nodes.statement_short: Prove (23) by disintegrating mu over the fibres.

nodes.name: Product measure and (24)
nodes.statement: Now define $\tilde{\mu}$:=$\nu\times\Leb$, the product measure on $\calL \times [0,1)$. We next prove that : \begin{equation} \Psi_{*}\tilde{\mu} = \mu. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define tilde mu = nu x Leb and announce Psi_* tilde mu = mu.

nodes.name: Verify (24) on rectangles
nodes.statement:
To see why \eqref{eqn:product_mes_push} holds, first note that the following collection of rectangles form a sub-base for $\Borel(L	imes [0,1))$. \[ \{R_{A,i,n}:=A	imes [ rac{i-1}{n}, rac{i}{n}) : \ A\in \Borel(L), \; n\in
um,\; 1\leq i \leq n \} \] Therefore, it is sufficient to prove \eqref{eqn:product_mes_push} for each such rectangle $R= R_{A,i,n}$. Each of the $n$ rectangles $R_{A,j,n}$ for $j=1,\ldots,n$, have the same $	ilde{\mu}$ measure $
u(A)/n$. Moreover, \[\Phi^{T/n} \left(\Psi(R_{A,j,n})ight) = \Psi(R_{A,j+1,n}),\quad  orall j=1,\ldots,n-1.\] Therefore, by the flow-invariance of $\mu$, \[\mu\left(\Psi(R_{A,j,n})ight) = \mu\left(\Phi^{T/n}\left(\Psi(R_{A,j,n})ight)ight) = \mu\left(\Psi(R_{A,j+1,n})ight).\] Therefore, all the images \{ $\Psi\left(R_{A,j,n}ight)$ : $j\in  races{1,\ldots,n}$ \} have the same $\mu$ measure. Therefore, \[ egin{gathered} \mu(\Psi\left(R_{A,j,n}ight)) =  rac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \mu \left( \Psi\left(R_{A,k,n}ight) ight) =  rac{1}{n} \mu \left( \Psi\left( \sqcup_{k=1}^{n} R_{A,k,n}ight) ight) =  rac{1}{n} \mu\left(\Psi\left(A	imes [0,1) ight)ight)\ \stackrel{	ext{by \eqref{eqn:product_mes_tower}}}{=}  rac{1}{n}
u(A) = 
u(A)	imes\Leb([ rac{j-1}{n}, rac{j}{n})) \stackrel{	ext{by definition}}{=} 	ilde{\mu}\left(R_{A,j,n}ight). \end{gathered}\] This completes the proof of \eqref{eqn:product_mes_push}.
nodes.statement_short: Check (24) on rectangles using flow invariance of mu.

nodes.name: phi is constant
nodes.statement: The proof of Claim~(iii) can now be completed. Fix an $A\subset L$ and set : \[ \phi:[0,1)\to\real, \quad \phi(s) := \paran{ \mu|\mathcal{F}_{2s\pi} } \paran{ \Phi^{sT}(A) }, \quad \forall s\in[0,1). \] The map $\phi$ is bounded and measurable. Next note that for every $[a,b)\subset [0,1)$, \[\begin{split} \frac{1}{b-a}\int_{a}^{b} \phi(t)dt &= \frac{1}{b-a} \int_{a}^{b} (\mu|\mathcal{F}_{2s\pi})(\Phi^{sT}(A)) ds = \frac{1}{b-a} \mu\left( \Psi(A\times[a,b]) \right) \\ &= \frac{1}{b-a}\tilde{\mu}\left(A\times [a,b]\right) \quad \mbox{[by \eqref{eqn:product_mes_push}]} \\ &= \nu(A) \equiv \mbox{constant}. \end{split}\] Thus the integral on the left hand side (LHS) is independent of the integration limits $a$ and $b$, which is possible if only if $\phi$ is a constant function. Therefore, we have shown that \begin{equation} \phi(s) = (\mu|\mathcal{F}_{2s\pi})(\Phi^{sT}(A)) = \nu(A) = \int_0^1 (\mu|\mathcal{F}_{2s\pi})(\Phi^{sT}(A)) ds, \quad \forall s\in [0,1). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Show the conditional mass function phi is constant, giving (25).

nodes.name: Conclude Claim (iii)
nodes.statement: Using this identity we can further say that \[\left( \Phi^{sT}_*(\mu | \calL_1) \right) (\Phi^{sT} A) = (\mu | \calL_1)(A) = \nu(A) = (\mu|\mathcal{F}_{2s\pi})(\Phi^{sT} A), \quad \forall A\in\Borel(L).\] The first equality follows from the definition of the push-forward of a measure. The last two equalities follow from \eqref{eqn:const_phi}. Since all sets in $\Borel(\mathcal{F}_{2s\pi})$ are of the form \{ $\Phi^{sT} A$ : $A\in\Borel(L)$ \}, the measures $\mu|\mathcal{F}_{2s\pi}$ and $\Phi^{sT}_*(\mu | \calL_1)$ must be the same and Claim~(iii) is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Push-forward of mu|L_1 equals the conditional measure on each fibre.

nodes.name: Claims (iv) and (v)
nodes.statement: To prove Claim~(iv), first note that by \eqref{eqn:const_phi}, $\mu|\calL_1 = \nu$. Thus the measure $\tilde{\mu}$ equals $\mu|\calL_1 \times \Leb$. So by \eqref{eqn:product_mes_push}, $\Psi_{*} (\mu|\calL_1 \times \Leb) = \mu$, as claimed. The fact that $\Psi$ is a continuous bijection follows from Claims (i) and (ii). The details of Claim (v) will be omitted as they are exactly analogous. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Claim (iv) from (25) and (24); (v) analogous.

nodes.name: Claim (i): conjugacy
nodes.statement: To prove Claim~(i), fix an arbitary point $(x,s)\in \calL_1 \times \real/\sim$. Without loss of generality (WLOG) we may assume that $0\leq s<1$. Then there is a unique integer $N$ such that $s+t-N\in [0,1)$. Then, \[\begin{split} \Psi\circ \Gamma^t (x,s) &= \Psi(R^N(x), s+t-N) = \Phi^{2\pi(s+t-N)/\omega} R^N(x) = \Phi^{2\pi(s+t-N)/\omega} \Phi^{2\pi N/\omega}(x) \\ & = \Phi^{2\pi(s+t)/\omega} (x)= \Phi^{2\pi t/\omega} \Phi^{2\pi s/\omega} (x) = \Phi^{2\pi t/\omega} \circ \Psi (x,s). \end{split}\] This confirms that $\Psi$ is indeed a conjugacy. The fact that it is a measure preserving conjugacy follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:fol_1D_basic}~(iv). This completes the proof of Claim (i).
nodes.statement_short: Compute Psi o Gamma^t directly; measure preservation from Theorem 1 (iv).

nodes.name: Claim (ii): base-map eigenfunction
nodes.statement: To prove Claim~(ii), fix $x\in \calL_1$, and use the fact that $\Psi$ is a conjugacy (by Claim (i) ) to observe that \[ \Psi(R(y),0) = \Phi^{2\pi/\omega}\Psi(y,0), \quad \forall y\in \calL_1. \] Then by the definition of $\tilde{\zeta}$ in \eqref{eqn:def:base_map}, \[ \tilde{\zeta} \left( R(x) \right) = \zeta\left( \Psi(R(x),0) \right) = \zeta \left( \Phi^{2\pi/\omega} \Psi(x,0) \right) = e^{\iota 2\pi \omega'/\omega} \zeta\left( \Psi(x,0)\right) = e^{\iota 2\pi \omega'/\omega} \tilde{\zeta} (x), \] as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Use the conjugacy to show tilde zeta o R = e^{i2pi omega'/omega} tilde zeta.

nodes.name: Claim (iii): extension
nodes.statement: To prove Claim~(iii), it has to be shown that for every $t>0$, every $x\in X$, $F\left( \Phi^{t} x \right)$ = $e^{\iota \omega' t} F(x)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:fol_1D_basic}~(ii), $\Psi$ is a bijection, so there is $y\in \calL_1$ and $s\in [0,1)$ such that $x= \Psi(y,s)$. Let $n\in\integer$ such that $r=\frac{\omega t}{2\pi} + s -n \in [0,1)$. Then claim (iii) follows from the following substitutions. \[\begin{split} \zeta \left( \Phi^t x \right) &= \zeta \left( \Phi^t \Psi(y,s) \right) = \zeta \left( \Phi^t \Phi^{2\pi s/\omega} y \right) = \zeta \left( \Phi^{2\pi r/\omega} \Phi^{2\pi n/\omega} y \right) = \zeta \left( \Phi^{2\pi r/\omega} R^{n} y \right) = \zeta \left( \Psi(R^{n}(y),r) \right)\\ & = e^{i 2\pi \omega' r/\omega} \tilde{\zeta} \paran{R^{n}(y)} = e^{i 2\pi \omega' r/\omega} e^{in2\pi \omega'/\omega} \tilde{\zeta}(y) = e^{ \iota 2 \pi \omega'(n+r)/\omega} \tilde{\zeta}(y) = e^{ \iota \omega' \paran{ t + s 2\pi/\omega } } \tilde{\zeta}(y) \\ & =e^{i \omega't} e^{ \iota 2 \pi \omega' s/\omega} \tilde{\zeta}(y) = e^{i \omega't} \zeta(\Psi(y,s)) = e^{i \omega't} \zeta(x). \\ \end{split}\] This completes the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:fol_1D_basemap}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Substitute x = Psi(y,s) to verify the eigenfunction equation for the extension.

nodes.name: Auxiliary lemma
nodes.statement:
We begin with a lemma that provides sufficient condition for a map to be strongly mixing.  egin{lemma} Let \{$\phi_k$ : $k\in
um$\} be a basis (not necessarily orthonormal) for $L^2(\mu)$, consisting of elements with uniformly bounded norm. Then  egin{enumerate} [(i)] \item the system is strongly mixing iff for every $i,j\in
um$, $\langle U^T \phi_i, \phi_j angle$ $	o 0$ as $T	o\infty$. \item If $\alpha:eal 	o eal$ is a positive function such that $\lim_{|T|	o\infty} \alpha(T)$ = $0$ and for every $i,j\in
um$, $\left| \langle \phi_i, U^T \phi_j angle_\mu ight| = O(\alpha(T))$. Then $\alpha$ is a rate of mixing for $F$. \end{enumerate} \end{lemma} Lemma ef{lem:mix_basis} is proved in Section ef{sec:proof:mix_basis}.
nodes.statement_short: State the lemma reducing mixing to a basis.

nodes.name: Choose generating frequencies
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{thm:fol_1D_return} is now ready to be proved. Let us set $m := \dim_{\Disc}$. Take $m$ independent frequencies $\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_m$ of the flow $\Phi^t$, with $\omega=\omega_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix m independent frequencies with omega_1 = omega.

nodes.name: Lower bound on eigenvalues of R
nodes.statement: Then by Theorem \ref{thm:fol_1D_basemap}, $e^{\iota 2\pi \omega_2/\omega}, \ldots, e^{\iota 2\pi \omega_m/\omega}$ are $m-1$ independent eigenvalues of the base map $R$. Thus the discrete subspace of $R$ has at least $m-1$ independent eigenvalues.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 2 gives m-1 independent eigenvalues of R.

nodes.name: Maximality, Claims (i) and (ii)
nodes.statement: We will show that this is a maximal set. Consider any eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $R$, it must be of the form $e^{\iota 2\pi \omega'/\omega}$ for some $\omega'\in\real$. Then by Theorem \ref{thm:fol_1D_basemap}~(iii), $\omega'$ is an eigenfrequency of $\Phi^t$. Thus there are integers $a_1, \ldots, a_m$ such that $\omega' = \sum_{i=1}^{m} a_i \omega_i$. Therefore \[ \lambda = \exp\left[ \frac{\iota 2\pi}{\omega} \sum_{i=1}^{m} a_i \omega_i \right] = \prod_{i=1}^{m} \left( e^{i a_i 2\pi\omega_i/\omega} \right)^{a_i} = \prod_{i=2}^{m} \left( e^{i a_i 2\pi\omega_i/\omega} \right)^{a_i}. \] The last equality follows from the fact that $\omega=\omega_1$. Thus $\lambda$ is generated by the $m-1$ eigenvalues, as claimed, proving Claim~(i). Claim (ii) is an immediate consequence of Claim~(i).
nodes.statement_short: Any eigenvalue of R comes from a flow eigenfrequency, so is generated by the m-1; (ii) follows.

nodes.name: Reduce to suspension flow
nodes.statement: By Claim~(i), the ergodic system $(\Phi^t,X,\mu)$ is measure theoretically isomorphic to a suspension flow $\Gamma^t$ from \eqref{eqn:def:susp_flow}. Therefore these two systems have the same ergodic properties and it is sufficient to prove Claim~(iii) for the suspension flow.
nodes.statement_short: Isomorphism reduces Claim (iii) to the suspension flow.

nodes.name: Rectangular functions
nodes.statement: To that end, we use a special class $\mathcal{R}$ of functions, called \emph{rectangular functions}, instead of general functions in $L^2(L,\nu\times \Leb)$. This class consists of functions of the form \[f(x,t) = 1_A(x)1_J(t),\] where $1_A$, $1_J$ are characteristic functions of Borel measurable sets $A\subset X$ and $J\subset [0,1]$. We can further restrict $J$ to be an interval. These functions have a dense span in $L^2(L,\nu\times \Leb)$ and by Lemma \ref{lem:mix_basis}, it suffices to check the mixing condition for such functions only.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to rectangular functions, enough by Lemma 3.

nodes.name: Image of rectangles under Gamma
nodes.statement: Let $f\in\mathcal{R}$. To simplify the analysis, we can assume without loss of generality that $f$ is of the form $A\times J$, with $J=[0,a)$ for some $a\in (0,1)$, and $A\in\Borel(L)$. Then, \[ \Gamma^{n+s}(A\times J) = \left\{ \begin{array}{lcl} R^n(A)\times [s,s+a) &\mbox{ for } &0\leq s<1-a \\ R^n(A)\times [s,1) \cup R^{n+1}(A)\times[0,a+s-1) &\mbox{ for } &1-a \leq s<1 \end{array} \right. \quad \forall n\in\integer, \forall s\in [0,1). \]
nodes.statement_short: Compute Gamma^{n+s} of a rectangle.

nodes.name: Correlations as convex sums
nodes.statement_short: Correlations of rectangular functions are convex sums of correlations of R.

nodes.name: Extend to all functions
nodes.statement: Both Claims (iii) and (iv) can now be seen to be true for rectangular functions, by virtue of \eqref{eqn:frhyt}. By Lemma \ref{lem:mix_basis}, they extend to all functions in $L^2(\nu\times\Leb)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3 extends the rectangular case to L^2.

nodes.name: Rate of mixing via truncation
nodes.statement_short: Truncate expansions to show correlations are O(alpha(T)).

nodes.name: Uniform bound and trivial direction
nodes.statement: We begin with the proof of Claim (i). Note that by assumption, $C$:= sup\{ $\|\phi_j\|$ : $j\in\num$\} is finite. The ``only if'' part is obvious.
nodes.statement_short: Set C = sup norm of the basis; the only-if part is obvious.

nodes.name: Converse setup
nodes.statement: So conversely, let for every $i,j\in\num$, $\langle U^T \phi_i, \phi_j \rangle$ $\to 0$ as $T\to\infty$. Let $f=\sum_{j\in\num} a_j \phi_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume basis correlations decay and expand f.

nodes.name: Decay against f
nodes.statement:
We first show that  egin{equation} \lim_{T	o\infty} \langle U^T \phi_i, f angle_\mu = 0, \quad  orall i\in
um . \end{equation} Let $\epsilon>0$. Choose $N\in
um$ large enough such that $\left\|\sum_{j=N+1}^{\infty} a_j \phi_j ight\| \leq \epsilon/C$. Then \[\left| \langle U^T \phi_i, f angle_\mu ight| = \left| \sum_{j\in
um}  ar{a_j} \langle U^T \phi_i, \phi_j angle_\mu ight| \leq \left| \sum_{j=1}^{N}  ar{a_j} \langle U^T \phi_i, \phi_j angle_\mu ight| + \left| \sum_{j=N+1}^{\infty} a_j\langle U^T \phi_i, \phi_j angle_\mu ight|.\] For $T$ large enough, by assumption on the $\phi_i$s, the first sum above becomes smaller than $\epsilon$. By the Cauchy Schwarz inequality and the fact that $U^T$ is a unitary operator, \[ \left| \sum_{j=N+1}^{\infty} a_j\langle U^T \phi_i, \phi_j angle_\mu ight| = \left| \sum_{j=N+1}^{\infty} a_j\langle \phi_i, U^{-T} \phi_j angle_\mu ight| = \left| \langle \phi_i,U^{-T} \sum_{j=N+1}^{\infty} a_j \phi_j angle_\mu ight| \leq \|\phi_i\| \left\|\sum_{j=N+1}^{\infty} a_j \phi_j ight\| < \epsilon .\] Therefore, the second sum is bounded by $\epsilon$. Thus for an arbitrary $\epsilon>0$, we have shown that $\left| \langle U^T \phi_i, f angle_\mu ight|<2\epsilon$. Thus \eqref{eqn:pof03} must be true.
nodes.statement_short: Show <U^T phi_i, f> -> 0.

nodes.name: Split the sum
nodes.statement: Let $\epsilon>0$. Choose $N\in\num$ large enough such that $\left\|\sum_{j=N+1}^{\infty} a_j \phi_j \right\| \leq \epsilon/C$. Then \[\left| \langle U^T \phi_i, f \rangle_\mu \right| = \left| \sum_{j\in\num} \bar{a_j} \langle U^T \phi_i, \phi_j \rangle_\mu \right| \leq \left| \sum_{j=1}^{N} \bar{a_j} \langle U^T \phi_i, \phi_j \rangle_\mu \right| + \left| \sum_{j=N+1}^{\infty} a_j\langle U^T \phi_i, \phi_j \rangle_\mu \right|.\]
nodes.statement_short: Choose N so the tail is small and split the sum.

nodes.name: Bound both parts
nodes.statement: For $T$ large enough, by assumption on the $\phi_i$s, the first sum above becomes smaller than $\epsilon$. By the Cauchy Schwarz inequality and the fact that $U^T$ is a unitary operator, \[ \left| \sum_{j=N+1}^{\infty} a_j\langle U^T \phi_i, \phi_j \rangle_\mu \right| = \left| \sum_{j=N+1}^{\infty} a_j\langle \phi_i, U^{-T} \phi_j \rangle_\mu \right| = \left| \langle \phi_i,U^{-T} \sum_{j=N+1}^{\infty} a_j \phi_j \rangle_\mu \right| \leq \|\phi_i\| \left\|\sum_{j=N+1}^{\infty} a_j \phi_j \right\| < \epsilon .\]
nodes.statement_short: Head small by hypothesis; tail small by Cauchy-Schwarz and unitarity.

nodes.name: Conclude (27)
nodes.statement: Therefore, the second sum is bounded by $\epsilon$. Thus for an arbitrary $\epsilon>0$, we have shown that $\left| \langle U^T \phi_i, f \rangle_\mu \right|<2\epsilon$. Thus \eqref{eqn:pof03} must be true.
nodes.statement_short: Both parts below epsilon gives (27).

nodes.name: Extend to all g and claim (ii)
nodes.statement: Now let $g=\sum_{i\in\num} b_i \phi_i$. In a manner exactly analogous to the steps above, it can be shown that $\lim_{T\to\infty} \langle U^T g, f \rangle$= 0. The second claim of the lemma also follows in a similar manner. This completes the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:mix_basis}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Analogous argument for general g, and for claim (ii).

nodes.name: Reduce (i) to orthogonality
nodes.statement: As shown in \citep[][Thm 2]{Das2023Lie} the gradient $\nabla_\tau z$ for such a submersion is orthogonal to the leaves of $\mathcal{F}$, with respect to (wrt) the $\tau$-metric. Thus Claim~(i) is equivalent to the identity $\langle \tilde{V}, \nabla_\tau z \rangle_\tau = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Gradient is normal to leaves, so (i) means <tilde V, grad z> = 0.

nodes.name: Compute inner products
nodes.statement:
By \eqref{def:grad_diff_Lie}, we have, \[ \iota \omega z = V z = \iota \langle V , 
abla_	au z angle_	au z \quad \Rightarrow \quad \langle V , 
abla_	au z angle_	au = \omega. \] Thus the inner product of $V$ with $
abla_	au z$ is constant everywhere in the $	au$-metric. Therefore, \[ \langle 	ilde{V}, 
abla_	au z angle_	au = \langle V, 
abla_	au z angle_	au - \omega \langle 
abla_	au z, 
abla_	au z angle_	au = \omega-\omega = 0 . \]
nodes.statement_short: <V, grad z> = omega, hence <tilde V, grad z> = 0.

nodes.name: Tangency of tilde V
nodes.statement: Thus $\tilde{V}$ is tangential to the leaves of $\mathcal{F}$. Since $z$ is constant on these leaves, $\tilde{V}(z) = 0$ everywhere, as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Hence tilde V is tangent and tilde V(z) = 0.

nodes.name: Scaling factor alpha
nodes.statement: We next prove Claim~(ii). Since the flow $\Phi^t$ preserves the leaves of the foliation, $\Phi^t_* TM \to TM$ preserves the sub-bundles $T\mathcal{F}$ and $T\mathcal{F}^\bot$. Thus there is a continuous function $\alpha:M\to\real$ such that \[\Phi^t_*|_x \nabla_\tau z(x) = \alpha(x) \nabla_\tau z(\Phi^t x), \quad \forall x\in M. \] It will be shown that $\alpha(x)\equiv 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Flow preserves normal bundle so push-forward of grad z is alpha times grad z.

nodes.name: alpha = 1
nodes.statement:
One of the fundamental facts from the theory of ordinary differential equations is that the flow $\Phi^t$ preserves the generating vector field $V$ :  egin{equation} V(\Phi^t(x)) = d/ds|_{s=t} \Phi^s(x) = d/ds|_{s=0} \Phi^{t+s}(x) = \Phi^t_* (x)V(x) . \end{equation} By the definition of $	ilde{V}(x)$, $V(x) = 	ilde{V}(x) + \omega 
abla_	au z(x)$. Therefore, \[ V(\Phi^t x) = \Phi^t_* (x)V(x) = \Phi^t_* (x)	ilde{V}(x) + \omega \alpha(x) 
abla_	au z(\Phi^t x). \] Taking inner products on both sides with $
abla_	au z(\Phi^t x)$ gives \[\omega = \langle V(\Phi^t x) , 
abla_	au z(\Phi^t x) angle_	au = \langle \Phi^t_* (x)	ilde{V}(x), 
abla_	au z(\Phi^t x) angle_	au + \omega \alpha(x) \langle
abla_	au z(\Phi^t x) , 
abla_	au z(\Phi^t x) angle_	au = 0 + \alpha\omega = \alpha\omega. \] Thus $\alpha=1$ as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Use invariance of V and inner products to get alpha = 1.

nodes.name: Invariance of tilde V
nodes.statement:
This means that the gradient vector field $
abla_	au z$ is invariant under the flow, namely, \[\Phi^t_*|_x 
abla_	au z(x) = 
abla_	au z(\Phi^t x), \quad  orall x\in M. \] Therefore, since $	ilde{V}$ is a linear combination of the two flow invariant vector fields $V$ and $
abla_	au z$, $	ilde{V}$ is also invariant under $\Phi^t$. We summarize all these invariances below.  egin{equation} \Phi^t_*|_x 	ilde{V}(x) = 	ilde{V}(\Phi^t x), \quad \Phi^t_*|_x V(x) = V(\Phi^t x), \quad \Phi^t_*|_x 
abla_	au z(x) = 
abla_	au z(\Phi^t x), \quad  orall x\in M. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: tilde V is a combination of invariant fields, hence invariant.

nodes.name: Commutation of flows
nodes.statement: We will next show that the two flows commute, i.e., $\tilde{\Phi}^t \Phi^s $ = $\Phi^s \tilde{\Phi}^{t}$ for every $s,t\in\real$. Let $x\in M$, and define $x'(s) := \tilde{\Phi}^s(x)$, $x''(s) := \Phi^t(x''(s))$ and $x'''(s) := \tilde{\Phi}^{-s}(x'(s))$. We have to show that $x'''(s) = \Phi^t(x)$ for every $s\in\real$. Since this is true for $s=0$, it is equivalent to prove that $\frac{d}{ds} x'''(s) = 0$. This follows from \[\begin{split} \frac{d}{ds} x'''(s) &= \frac{d}{ds} \tilde{\Phi}^{-s} \Phi^t \tilde{\Phi}^s(x) = \frac{d}{du}|_{u=s} \tilde{\Phi}^{-u} \Phi^t \tilde{\Phi}^s(x) + \frac{d}{dv}|_{v=s} \tilde{\Phi}^{-s} \Phi^t \tilde{\Phi}^v(x) \\ &= -\tilde{V}(x'''(s)) + \tilde{\Phi}^{-s}_*|_{x''(s)} \Phi^t_*|_{x'(s)} \tilde{V}(x'(s)) \\ & = -\tilde{V}(x'''(s)) + \tilde{\Phi}^{-s}_*|_{x''(s)} \tilde{V}(x''(s)), \quad \mbox{by } \eqref{eqn:inv_vector}, \\ & = -\tilde{V}(x'''(s)) + \tilde{V}(x'''(s)) = 0. \end{split}\] The last equality above again follows from the invariance of the vector field $\tilde{V}$ under the flow $\tilde{\Phi}^t$ that it generates. This completes the proof of Claim~(ii). This completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:fol_1D_flow}. See Figure~\ref{fig:comm_flow} for an illustration. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the conjugated flow in s to show the flows commute.

nodes.name: Claim (i) omitted
nodes.statement: The proof of Claim~(i) is analogous to the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:fol_1D_basic}~(iii), and will be omitted.
nodes.statement_short: Claim (i) is analogous to Theorem 1 (iii).

nodes.name: Eigenvalue equation for the extension
nodes.statement: We next prove Claim~(iv). By \eqref{def:tildeV} we have \[ V \zeta = \tilde{V} \zeta + \omega \nabla_\tau z \zeta . \] The first differential operator acts only along the tangent subspaces of the leaves of $z$. The second differential operator acts along the vector field normal to the flow. Due to the local product structure, \[ V \zeta = \iota \omega' \zeta + \iota \omega z \zeta . \] Thus $\zeta$ satisfies the eigenfunction equation with eigenfrequency $\omega + \omega'$.
nodes.statement_short: Split V zeta into tangential and normal parts to get eigenfrequency omega+omega'.

nodes.name: Regularity classes
nodes.statement: If $\tilde\zeta$ is a $C^r$ eigenfunction, then so is $\zeta$. Suppose $\tilde\zeta$ is an $L^2(\tilde{\mu})$ eigenfunction. By Theorem \ref{thm:fol_1D_basic}~(iii) , since the flow $\Phi^t$ preserves the conditional measures of $\mu$ along the fibres of $\mathcal{F}$, the set $M'$ on which the eigenvalue equation holds has full $\mu$-measure. Thus, $\zeta$ is an $L^2(\mu)$ eigenfunction.
nodes.statement_short: C^r case immediate; L^2 case from Theorem 1 (iii).

nodes.name: Claim (iii): orthonormal gradients
nodes.statement:
By Lemma ef{lem:submersion}, the $d$ vector fields $
abla_	au z_1, \ldots, 
abla_	au z_d$ are linearly independent everywhere on $M$, for any choice of a Riemannian metric $	au$. Thus $	au$ can be chosen so that these vector fields are mutually orthogonal and each of constant unit norm. As a result, using the identity \eqref{def:grad_diff_Lie} for the gradient, we get \[ 	ilde{V}(z_j) = V(z_j) - \omega 
abla_{	au} z_1(z_j) = \iota \omega_j z_j - i \omega \langle 
abla_{	au} z_1 , 
abla_{	au} z_j angle_{	au} z_j = \iota \omega_j z_j, \quad j=2,\ldots,d . \] This completes the proof of Claim~(iii) and of Theorem~ef{thm:fol_1D_flow_eig}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 1 lets tau make gradients orthonormal, so tilde V(z_j) = i omega_j z_j.
